blocks.text: A sequence of numbers is called a Harmonic Sequence or Harmonic Progression (H.P.) if the reciprocals of its terms are in arithmetic progression. The sequence \(1, \frac{1}{3}, \frac{1}{5}, \frac{1}{7}\) is a harmonic sequence since their reciprocals \(1, 3, 5, 7\) are in A.P.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
The reciprocal of a number \(x\) is \(\frac{1}{x}\): we simply turn the fraction upside down. The reciprocal of \(\frac{1}{3}\) is \(3\), and the reciprocal of \(5\) is \(\frac{1}{5}\).
So an H.P. is not a new kind of pattern with its own formulas: it is an A.P. written upside down. In \(1, \frac{1}{3}, \frac{1}{5}, \frac{1}{7}\) the terms themselves do not have a common difference (\(\frac{1}{3} - 1 = -\frac{2}{3}\) but \(\frac{1}{5} - \frac{1}{3} = -\frac{2}{15}\)), yet their reciprocals \(1, 3, 5, 7\) increase by \(2\) each time.
Every H.P. question is therefore solved in three moves: (1) take reciprocals to get an A.P., (2) work in the A.P. with the formulas you already know, (3) take reciprocals again to come back to the H.P.
Remember that the reciprocal of zero is not defined, so zero cannot be the term of a harmonic sequence.
The general form of a harmonic sequence is taken as:

blocks.text_alt: 1 over a 1, 1 over (a 1 plus d), 1 over (a 1 plus 2 d), and so on
T n equals 1 over (a 1 plus (n minus 1) d)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Here \(a_{1}\) and \(d\) are the first term and the common difference of the corresponding A.P. (the A.P. of reciprocals), not of the H.P. itself.
The formula is just the A.P. formula \(a_{n} = a_{1} + (n-1)d\) put in the denominator: find the \(n^{\text{th}}\) term of the A.P., then take its reciprocal.
Because zero is never a term, no term \(a_{1} + (n-1)d\) of the A.P. may be zero.

blocks.title: Example 23
blocks.problem: Find the \(n^{\text{th}}\) and \(8^{\text{th}}\) terms of H.P.: \(\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{5}, \frac{1}{8}, \dots\)
steps:
Given: the H.P. \(\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{5}, \frac{1}{8}, \dots\)
To find: its \(n^{\text{th}}\) term and its \(8^{\text{th}}\) term.
Method: an H.P. has no term formula of its own, so we take reciprocals to get an A.P., find the A.P.'s \(n^{\text{th}}\) term with \(a_{n} = a_{1} + (n-1)d\), and take the reciprocal back.

Step 1: Take the reciprocals of the terms
\[\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{5}, \frac{1}{8}, \dots \ \to\ 2, 5, 8, \dots\]
Why: by definition the reciprocals of the terms of an H.P. are in A.P., and we know how to handle an A.P.

Step 2: First term and common difference of the A.P.
\[a_{1} = 2\]
\[d = 5 - 2 = 3\]
Why: \(d\) is any term minus the term before it. (The book prints this line as \(d = 5 \;\; 2 = 3\); the minus sign is missing, see the correction below.)

Step 3: The \(n^{\text{th}}\) term of the A.P.
\[a_{n} = a_{1} + (n-1)d\]
\[a_{n} = 2 + (n-1)3\]
\[= 2 + 3n - 3\]
\[a_{n} = 3n - 1\]
Why: we put \(a_{1} = 2\) and \(d = 3\) into the A.P. formula and open the bracket.

Step 4: The \(n^{\text{th}}\) term of the H.P.
\[T_{n} = \dfrac{1}{a_{n}} = \dfrac{1}{3n-1}\]
Why: each H.P. term is the reciprocal of the A.P. term in the same position.

Step 5: The \(8^{\text{th}}\) term
\[T_{8} = \dfrac{1}{3 \times 8 - 1}\]
\[= \dfrac{1}{23}\]
Why: put \(n = 8\) in the \(n^{\text{th}}\) term found in Step 4.

Step 6: The book's alternative way
\[a_{8} = a_{1} + (8-1)d\]
\[= 2 + 7(3) = 23\]
\[T_{8} = \dfrac{1}{23}\]
Why: if only one term is needed, we can find that A.P. term directly and take its reciprocal.

Check:
\(n = 1\): \(\frac{1}{3(1)-1} = \frac{1}{2}\); \(n = 2\): \(\frac{1}{5}\); \(n = 3\): \(\frac{1}{8}\). The formula gives the three printed terms, so it is right.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In the solution of Example 23 the book prints \(d = 5 \;\; 2 = 3\): the minus sign is missing. It should read \(d = 5 - 2 = 3\).

blocks.title: Example 24
blocks.problem: If the \(4^{\text{th}}\) term and \(7^{\text{th}}\) term of the H.P. are \(\frac{2}{13}\) and \(\frac{2}{25}\) respectively, find the sequence.
steps:
Given: in an H.P., \(T_{4} = \frac{2}{13}\) and \(T_{7} = \frac{2}{25}\).
To find: the sequence (its first few terms).
Method: turn the two H.P. terms into the corresponding A.P. terms, write each as \(a_{1} + (n-1)d\), solve the two equations for \(a_{1}\) and \(d\), build the A.P. and take reciprocals.

Step 1: Terms of the corresponding A.P.
\[a_{4} = \dfrac{13}{2},\quad a_{7} = \dfrac{25}{2}\]
Why: the reciprocal of \(\frac{2}{13}\) is \(\frac{13}{2}\) and of \(\frac{2}{25}\) is \(\frac{25}{2}\); the reciprocals of an H.P. form an A.P.

Step 2: Write two equations
\[a_{1} + 3d = \dfrac{13}{2} \quad \text{(i)}\]
\[a_{1} + 6d = \dfrac{25}{2} \quad \text{(ii)}\]
Why: \(a_{4} = a_{1} + (4-1)d\) and \(a_{7} = a_{1} + (7-1)d\). Two unknowns need two equations.

Step 3: Subtract (i) from (ii)
\[3d = \dfrac{25}{2} - \dfrac{13}{2} = 6\]
\[d = 2\]
Why: subtracting removes \(a_{1}\), leaving one equation in \(d\) only.

Step 4: Find \(a_{1}\) from (i)
\[a_{1} = \dfrac{13}{2} - 3d\]
\[= \dfrac{13}{2} - 6 = \dfrac{1}{2}\]
Why: once \(d\) is known, either equation gives \(a_{1}\).

Step 5: Next terms of the A.P.
\[a_{2} = a_{1} + d = \dfrac{1}{2} + 2 = \dfrac{5}{2}\]
\[a_{3} = a_{1} + 2d = \dfrac{1}{2} + 4 = \dfrac{9}{2}\]
and \(a_{4} = \frac{13}{2}\) is given.
Why: each A.P. term is the previous one plus \(d = 2\).

Step 6: Take reciprocals to get the H.P.
\[\dfrac{2}{1}, \dfrac{2}{5}, \dfrac{2}{9}, \dfrac{2}{13}, \dots\]
Why: we return from the A.P. to the H.P. by turning each term upside down. (\(\frac{2}{1}\) is simply \(2\).)

Check:
\[a_{7} = \dfrac{1}{2} + 6(2) = \dfrac{25}{2}\]
so \(T_{7} = \frac{2}{25}\), as given; and \(T_{4} = \frac{2}{13}\) appears in our list.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Numbers are in H.P. when their reciprocals are in A.P.
2. Zero can never be a term of an H.P.
3. \(n^{\text{th}}\) term: \(T_{n} = \frac{1}{a_{1} + (n-1)d}\), where \(a_{1}\), \(d\) belong to the A.P. of reciprocals.
4. Method: flip to an A.P., work there, flip back.
5. Check by putting \(n = 1, 2, 3\) into your answer.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Looking for a common difference in the H.P. terms themselves: \(\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{5}, \frac{1}{8}\) have no common difference; only their reciprocals do.
2. Forgetting to flip back: in Example 23 the A.P. term is \(23\), but the H.P. term is \(\frac{1}{23}\).
3. Writing the reciprocal of \(\frac{2}{13}\) as \(\frac{1}{13}\) or \(13\): the whole fraction turns over, giving \(\frac{13}{2}\).
4. Using \(\frac{1}{a_{1}} + (n-1)d\) instead of \(\frac{1}{a_{1} + (n-1)d}\): the whole A.P. term goes in the denominator.
